Acinonyx jubatus hecki.note: The critically endangered Saharan cheetah, ranging vast arid territories.

Addax nasomaculatus.note: The addax, an antelope that can live without drinking free water.

Aegyptopithecus.note: A Fayum catarrhine near the base of the Old World monkey and ape split.

Aepycamelus.note: A giraffe-necked camel browsing the tall Miocene savanna of the plains.

Alces.note: The moose: the largest deer, browsing willow and feeding in boreal lakes, its splayed hooves suited to bog and snow.

Alces alces.note: The moose: the largest deer, browsing willow and feeding in boreal lakes and bogs.

Ambulocetus.note: The 'walking whale' of Indo-Pakistani Eocene coasts, a crocodile-like stage in whale origins.

Antilocapra.note: The pronghorn: sole survivor of a family found nowhere but North America, and still fast enough to outrun a predator that has been extinct for 10,000 years.

Antilocapra americana.note: The pronghorn, still outrunning a predator that went extinct 12,000 years ago.

Archaeoceti.note: The early whales, from four-legged waders to the fully marine, serpent-bodied Basilosaurus of warm Eocene seas.

Arsinoitherium.note: A rhino-like herbivore with two enormous horns, endemic to the Fayum swamps.

Astrapotherium.note: A tapir-like endemic ungulate of the Santa Cruz beds of Patagonia.

Australopithecus.note: Small-brained, upright-walking hominins; the Laetoli trackway in Tanzania records them walking through volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago.

Australopithecus afarensis.note: Lucy's species: bipedal, small-brained, and the maker of the Laetoli footprint trail.

Balaena mysticetus.note: The bowhead whale, adapted to break sea ice, is the signature large animal of the modern Arctic.

Balaenoptera musculus.note: The blue whale, the largest animal that has ever lived, reaching that size only in the productive oceans of the ice ages.

Basilosaurus.note: An eighteen-metre fully aquatic archaeocete with vestigial hind limbs, preserved by the hundred at Wadi Al-Hitan.
Basilosaurus.hb: fully aquatic, serpentine, with vestigial hindlimbs

Bison.note: Bison: steppe grazers that arose in Eurasia and crossed Beringia in the Ice Age; they survive as the American bison and the European wisent.

Bison bison.note: The American bison, whose herds shaped the whole grassland before 1870.
Bison bison.conf_note: PBDB-robust 1.3 Ma reflects the ancestral Asian Bison population; B. bison specifically crossed into North America only ~0.2 Ma.

Bison priscus.note: The steppe bison, ranging the land bridge between continents.

Bos mutus.note: The wild yak, dense-coated for the plateau's thin cold air.

Cambaytherium.note: A Vastan lignite mammal near the root of odd-toed ungulates, recording India's brief faunal isolation.

Camelus.note: Camels -- which evolved in North America and only later reached the deserts they are now the emblem of.

Camelus ferus.note: The wild Bactrian camel, drinking salt water no other large mammal tolerates.

Canis dirus.note: The dire wolf, the commonest large carnivore in the La Brea tar.

Canis lupus.note: The grey wolf, once the most widely distributed wild land mammal on Earth.

Canis simensis.note: The Ethiopian wolf, Africa's rarest carnivore, hunting Afroalpine rodents.

Capra ibex.note: The Alpine ibex, grazing near-vertical rock.

Carpolestes.note: A small primate relative with a grasping foot and a nail in place of a claw: the beginning of primate hands.

Castorocauda lutrasimilis.note: A beaver-tailed, swimming mammaliaform with preserved fur -- evidence Jurassic mammals were not all generic shrews.

Cebus.note: A New World capuchin monkey, among the most familiar living platyrrhines.

Cervus.note: Red deer and their relatives, the characteristic large browsers of the Palearctic woodland and steppe.

Cetacea.note: Whales and dolphins: hoofed mammals that returned to the sea in the Eocene and became its largest predators and filter-feeders.

Chrysocyon brachyurus.note: The maned wolf, long-legged for seeing over cerrado grass.

Coelodonta antiquitatis.note: The woolly rhinoceros, its appearance known from cave paintings as well as bones.

Condylarthra.note: A wastebasket of archaic hoofed mammals from which most modern ungulate groups eventually emerge.

Connochaetes taurinus.note: The blue wildebeest, whose migration is the largest surviving land-mammal movement.

Cynomys ludovicianus.note: Black-tailed prairie dogs, whose towns are the grassland's keystone.

Darwinius masillae.note: An exquisitely complete Messel primate, gut contents and all, from near the base of the primate radiation.

Deinotherium.note: A proboscidean with downward-curving lower tusks, unrelated to any surviving elephant lineage.

Diprotodon.note: A three-tonne wombat relative, the largest marsupial ever, gone from Australia around 46,000 years ago.

Docodonta.note: Small mammaliaforms with complex molars, exploiting insect and plant food in the dinosaurs' shadow.

Doedicurus.note: A glyptodont with a spiked tail-club, among the largest of the armoured Ice Age herbivores.

Ectoconus.note: A sheep-sized archaic hoofed mammal typifying the Paleocene recovery fauna of the western basins.

Elephas.note: The Asian elephant lineage, which arose in Africa about five million years ago and spread across southern Asia.

Enaliarctos.note: An early pinniped, at the transition of carnivorans into fully marine life.

Entelodontidae.note: 'Hell pigs': massive omnivorous artiodactyls with metre-long skulls, bony cheek flanges and bone-crushing jaws.

Eohippus.note: The 'dawn horse', a dog-sized browser of Eocene woodlands, the base of the classic horse lineage.

Equus.note: Horses and zebras. Their high-crowned teeth and single toe are the standard example of an animal rebuilt by the spread of grass.

Equus ferus.note: The wild horse, the steppe's defining grazer.

Fennecus zerda.note: The fennec fox, radiating heat through outsized ears.

Glyptodon.note: An armoured, car-sized relative of armadillos, native to South America -- the interchange traveller into North America was its relative Glyptotherium.
Glyptodon.conf_note: Draft raw range (36-0) is a bin artefact; NA/CA occurrences likely reflect Glyptotherium, not Glyptodon.

Gorilla gorilla.note: The western gorilla, a folivore of dense secondary forest.

Gulo.note: The wolverine: a mustelid that kills prey many times its size and caches it in the frozen ground.

Gulo gulo.note: The wolverine: a mustelid that kills prey many times its size and caches it in the frozen ground.

Hipparion.note: A three-toed grazing horse whose rapid spread across the Old World is a datable event in its own right.

Hippocamelus bisulcus.note: The huemul, a stocky Andean deer of the southern forests.

Hippopotamus amphibius.note: The hippopotamus, whose nightly paths and wallows engineer the channels of African wetlands.

Homo erectus.note: The first truly wide-ranging human, out of Africa by about 1.8 million years ago and across southern Asia -- the hominin present through most of the Pleistocene, long before our own species.

Homo habilis.note: Associated with the earliest widely accepted stone tool industries, right at the interval's close.

Homo neanderthalensis.note: The cold-adapted human of Ice Age Europe and western Asia, from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago, overlapping and interbreeding with our species before vanishing.
Homo neanderthalensis.conf_note: PBDB lad (0.011) mismatches the real Neanderthal extinction ~40 ka; matches the existing note.

Homo sapiens.note: Our species. It arose in Africa around 300,000 years ago, spread across Eurasia after about 70,000, reached Australia by 65,000 and the Americas by 20,000 -- so before that it was nowhere, and the map should not show it.
Homo sapiens.conf_note: PBDB fad (1.3 Ma) is a bin artefact; real origin ~300 ka in Africa, matching the existing note.

Hyaenodon.note: A hypercarnivorous hyaenodont with slicing cheek teeth, a leading predator of the northern continents from the Eocene to the Miocene.

Hyracotherium.note: The dog-sized ancestral horse, browsing in closed forest on four toes.

Icaronycteris.note: An early bat from Green River with fully modern wings and evidence of echolocation.

Inia geoffrensis.note: The Amazon river dolphin, pink-skinned and flexible enough to hunt in flooded forest.

Lemmus.note: Lemmings, whose population cycles drive the whole tundra food web.

Litopterna.note: Endemic hoofed mammals, some convergent on horses and camels, unique to South America.

Loxodonta.note: The African elephant, and the reason the Afrotropical realm still has an intact large-mammal fauna when every other realm lost one.

Loxodonta africana.note: The African bush elephant, whose feeding keeps the savanna from closing to woodland.

Macrauchenia.note: A camel-bodied, trunk-nosed litoptern, one of the last of the endemic ungulates.

Macropodidae.note: Kangaroos radiate as grasslands spread across the drying interior.

Mammut.note: The American mastodon, a forest browser arriving as Pliocene climate cooled.

Mammuthus.note: Mammoths spread across the newly cold northern continents as the mammoth steppe forms.
Mammuthus.conf_note: Africa 5 Ma -> Eurasia 3 Ma -> North America 1.5 Ma.

Mammuthus columbi.note: The Columbian mammoth, the largest Ice Age grazer of the North American plains.

Mammuthus primigenius.note: The woolly mammoth, keystone grazer of the mammoth steppe, surviving on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.
Mammuthus primigenius.hb: cold-adapted grazer of the mammoth steppe
Mammuthus primigenius.conf_note: Species origin ~400 ka; PBDB fad reflects the ancestral trogontherii lineage. Wrangel Island survival to 4 ka matches the existing note.

Marmota bobak.note: The bobak marmot, whose burrowing turns over the steppe soil.

Marmota marmota.note: The Alpine marmot, hibernating eight months of the year.

Megacerops.note: A massive brontothere with a forked nasal horn, abundant in the White River badlands and extinct by the mid-Oligocene.

Megalonyx.note: A ground sloth whose ancestors rafted into North America in the late Miocene, well before the Isthmus of Panama existed; gave rise to Megalonyx jeffersonii of the Ice Age.

Megatherium.note: A ground sloth the size of an elephant, rearing up to pull down branches.
Megatherium.hb: terrestrial browser, able to rear on its hindlimbs
Megatherium.conf_note: PBDB fad inflated by coarse bins; real fad ~5.3 Ma. NA/CA occurrences are likely Eremotherium, a different genus.

Merychippus.note: A three-toed grazing horse of the spreading Miocene Great Plains grasslands.

Merycoidodon.note: The 'oreodont', a sheep-like cud-chewer so abundant it defines the White River badlands fauna.

Mesohippus.note: A three-toed horse with teeth intermediate between browsing and grazing, tracking the opening landscape.

Moeritherium.note: A pig-sized, semi-aquatic early proboscidean - a distant, low-slung ancestor of elephants.

Morganucodon.note: A shrew-sized nocturnal insectivore with a mammalian jaw joint -- close to the origin of mammals.

Multituberculata.note: Rodent-like mammals that had thrived alongside dinosaurs and now briefly dominate, before rodents outcompete them.

Myrmecophaga tridactyla.note: The giant anteater, tearing open termite mounds with its foreclaws and feeding with a sixty-centimetre tongue.

Mysticeti.note: Baleen whales reach modern size as intensified coastal upwelling concentrates their food into dense patches.

Nimbadon.note: A sheep-sized tree-dwelling marsupial herbivore, mass-preserved in Riversleigh cave pools.

Notoryctes typhlops.note: The marsupial mole, blind and swimming through sand.

Notoungulata.note: An endemic order of South American hoofed mammals that evolved in continental isolation.

Obdurodon.note: A Riversleigh platypus that, unlike the living one, kept functional teeth as an adult.

Okapia johnstoni.note: The okapi, the giraffe family's last forest-dwelling member, confined to the Ituri rainforest of the Congo.

Oreamnos americanus.note: The mountain goat, on cliffs no predator can follow.

Oryx.note: Desert antelope able to let their body temperature rise through the day rather than spend water cooling it.

Oryx gazella.note: The gemsbok, tolerating body temperatures that would kill most mammals.

Ovibos.note: The muskox, a survivor of the Pleistocene mammoth steppe that rings its calves with horns against wolves.

Ovibos moschatus.note: The muskox, a survivor of the Pleistocene mammoth steppe.

Ovis nivicola.note: The snow sheep, isolated on the range's high plateaus.

Panthera.note: The big roaring cats: lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar. Ambush predators that track the large herbivores of each continent.

Panthera leo.note: The lion, the only truly social big cat.

Panthera onca.note: The jaguar, the Americas' largest cat and the forest's apex predator.

Panthera spelaea.note: The cave lion, hunting across Beringia's cold grassland.

Panthera uncia.note: The snow leopard, hunting blue sheep across cliff and scree.

Pantholops hodgsonii.note: The chiru, migrating hundreds of km across the plateau to calve.

Paraceratherium.note: A hornless rhinocerotoid five metres at the shoulder and around twenty tonnes -- the largest land mammal known.
Paraceratherium.conf_note: EXTANT tag is a coarse-bin artefact; extinct by early Miocene.

Paranthropus boisei.note: A heavily-built, small-brained hominin of eastern Africa with huge grinding molars, sharing the early Pleistocene with the first members of Homo.

Platyrrhini.note: New World monkeys, arriving in South America by transatlantic rafting and radiating in isolation.

Plesiadapiformes.note: Squirrel-like early primate relatives, arboreal and probably nocturnal.

Polydolopidae.note: Marsupials on Seymour Island, recording the old land connection between Antarctica, South America and Australia.

Proconsul.note: An early African ape without a tail, near the base of the hominoid radiation.

Procoptodon.note: A short-faced giant kangaroo browsing shrubs on one-toed feet.

Propalaeotherium.note: A small Eocene browsing horse relative, found at Messel with leaves still in its stomach.

Pseudois nayaur.note: The bharal, the snow leopard's principal prey.

Ptilodus.note: A Paleocene multituberculate with an enlarged shearing premolar and an opposable-like hind toe.

Purgatorius.note: A small mammal at or near the base of the primate lineage, appearing right at the boundary.

Pyrotherium.note: An elephant-like endemic ungulate of the Oligocene Salla and Deseado faunas.

Rangifer.note: Reindeer: the only deer where both sexes carry antlers, and the large herbivore that makes tundra a grazed system rather than a frozen one.

Rangifer tarandus.note: Reindeer or caribou, the only deer in which both sexes carry antlers, grazing lichen through the northern winter.

Repenomamus.note: A badger-sized Jehol mammal found with a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach -- Mesozoic mammals were not all prey.

Sahelanthropus.note: A late-Miocene Chadian hominin near the split of the human and chimpanzee lines.

Sahelanthropus tchadensis.note: A Chadian skull around seven million years old, close to the chimpanzee-human split and arguably on our side of it.

Saiga tatarica.note: The saiga, its bulbous nose filtering dust and warming winter air.
Saiga tatarica.conf_note: PBDB-robust n=4 is thin; Saiga's Eurasian mammoth-steppe record starts in the Early Pleistocene, well before 0.452 Ma; living range split into a Pleistocene Beringian lobe (na-n, as-n) and the present Eurasian remnant (eu, as-c).

Sirenia.note: Dugongs and manatees: the only plant-eating marine mammals, grazing seagrass meadows of warm shallow shelves.

Sivapithecus.note: A large Miocene ape from the Siwaliks, close to the ancestry of the orangutan.

Smilodon.note: The sabre-toothed cat, moving south into a South America that had never seen anything like it.
Smilodon.conf_note: NA origin ~2.5 Ma; South America only after GABI, ~1 Ma.

Smilodon fatalis.note: The Rancho La Brea sabre-tooth, known from thousands of individuals trapped in asphalt seeps.

Sparassodonta.note: Marsupial-relative carnivores that filled the cat-and-dog roles on the island continent.

Stegodon.note: A large proboscidean with tusks set so close together that the trunk hung to one side; its dwarfed island forms reached Flores and Timor.

Teleoceras.note: A hippo-like short-legged rhino that wallowed in Miocene rivers, mass-buried at Ashfall.

Thalassocnus.note: A marine ground sloth that grazed seagrass off the Peruvian coast -- a lineage no one predicted.
Thalassocnus.conf_note: PBDB collections are the Pisco coast of Peru; the range is that coast's ocean, by design

Theropithecus gelada.note: The gelada, the last grass-eating primate, endemic to these escarpments.

Thylacoleo.note: Early marsupial 'lions' with bolt-cutter premolars appear in the Miocene rainforest fauna.

Thylacoleo carnifex.note: The marsupial lion, a powerful ambush predator with the strongest bite of any known mammal for its size.

Toxodon.note: One of the endemic South American ungulate orders that the interchange extinguished.
Toxodon.hb: heavy grazer, rhinoceros-like in build but unrelated

Uintatherium.note: A rhino-sized herbivore with six blunt horns and sabre-like canines, belonging to no surviving group.
Uintatherium.hb: heavy browser with six blunt horns

Ursus.note: Bears. Omnivorous, wide-ranging, and one of the few large carnivores that hibernates through a boreal winter.

Ursus americanus.note: The American black bear, the range's largest surviving carnivore.

Ursus arctos horribilis.note: The grizzly, ranging from valley floor to alpine tundra.

Ursus spelaeus.note: The cave bear, whose bones fill Ice Age European caverns by the thousand.

Vicugna vicugna.note: The vicuna, grazing the altiplano on the finest wool of any mammal.

Volaticotherium.note: A gliding mammaliaform with a preserved membrane, roughly 100 million years before bats.

Vulpes lagopus.note: The Arctic fox, changing coat colour with the season.

primates.note: Grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains -- a group built by and largely confined to closed forest canopy.
